Work a job, from template to final report

John Ehrlinger

Source: vignettes/work-a-job.qmd

Every analysis in a study is a job: one Quarto file that reads the study’s data, runs one piece of the analysis, and renders a report. You start a job from a template, change the lines the template cannot know about your study, and render it. This guide walks that loop once, in the order you meet it, and says what to do when the job stops you.

It assumes the study already exists and has its dataset registered. If it does not, start with Start a new study, or with Adopt an existing study for a study that already has a folder of SAS jobs. Everything below is typed in the R console of the study’s RStudio Project.

Which template do I want?

Start at the template gallery. It lists every template the package ships, says in a sentence what each one is for, and opens the report each one produces on a synthetic study, so you can see the tables and figures before you commit to a job. If you knew the SAS job by its name, dc.gfup.sas say, look for the same letters: the R template keeps the prefix (dc) and the job type (gfup).

The same list is in R. template_list() returns one row per template:

library(hvtiRtemplates)
tl <- template_list()
tl[, c("name", "folder", "call")]

The call column is the line that adds the template to your study. To find the follow-up jobs, ask for their job type:

subset(tl, qualifier == "gfup", c(name, folder, call))

Two templates come back. dc.gfup is the one to use; dp.gfup still works but is deprecated, and says so with a warning when you add it.

Add it to the study

Copy the call, and change two words before you run it:

add_job("dc.gfup", subject = "cohort", type = "eda")

subject and type name your job, not the template. Together they say which set of work the job belongs to: here, exploratory checks (eda) on the whole cohort (cohort). A job modeling death might be subject = "dead", type = "hz". Use letters, digits and underscores only, because the two words become part of the filename.

The job lands in the folder the template belongs in, named <template>.<subject>.<type>.qmd, so the line above writes 10_descriptive/dc.gfup.cohort.eda.qmd (or descriptive/... in a study that kept the older, unnumbered folder names). add_job() never overwrites a job that already exists, because a job collects your edits. To open a job, creating it first if it is not there yet, use open_job() with the same arguments; it opens the file in RStudio.

job <- open_job("dc.gfup", subject = "cohort", type = "eda")

Find what you have to change

A new job is not finished. Every line the template cannot fill in for your study carries an EDIT: marker: a comment saying what to set and why it matters. The dataset to read, the event and follow-up columns, the origin year of the operation-year interval, and so on. The job is finished when no marker is left.

There are three ways to find them.

The report tells you. Render the job (next section) and the top of the report carries a DRAFT banner listing every marker still in the file, with the first words of each line. A new dc-gfup job starts with sixteen:

16 unresolved EDIT: marker(s) remain in this job:
  - <!-- EDIT: name the job this replaces (descriptive/dc.gfup). -->
  - # EDIT: the registered dataset this job reads ("built" is the study dataset).
  - # EDIT: an hvtiRdatabuild analysis set, or NULL to read the whole dataset.
  ...

RStudio finds them. With the job open, press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac), type EDIT: and step through the matches with Enter. In most templates the bulk of them sit together under the heading Study choices, near the top, so most of the work is in one place.

The console lists them, with line numbers. This prints the line number and text of each marker left in the job, which is handy for a long job:

lines <- readLines(job)
hits <- grep("EDIT:", lines, fixed = TRUE)
data.frame(line = hits, text = trimws(lines[hits]))

Work each marker: set the value, then delete the word EDIT: (or the whole comment, if it no longer says anything you need). Read the comment before you delete it. Several say why a choice matters, and a few name a mistake that otherwise fails quietly, such as an origin year that slides every point along the axis without any other symptom.

Render as you go

You do not have to finish the markers before you render. Render early and often:

render_job(job)

That is a draft render. It runs the whole job from top to bottom in a clean R session, writes the HTML report beside the job, and shows the DRAFT banner while any marker remains. The numbers in a draft are not a result, and the banner says so.

Render the job; do not run its chunks by hand. Run All in RStudio runs the chunks in your current R session, where an object you made an hour ago, or a setting left by another job you had open, can quietly stand in for one this job no longer makes. Every job uses the same setting names (DATASET, WHERE, VARIABLES and the rest), so a stale one reads the wrong patients and nothing says so. A render starts from nothing, so every number in it comes from this job. To look at the data while you set the choices, render a draft and read the report: it shows the selection, its counts and the tables. To see only the top of a long job, put stop_here() below the part you are working on, and the render stops there.

When the markers are gone and the report says what it should, render the final:

render_job(job, final = TRUE)

A final render is the accepted result. It refuses to finish while any EDIT: marker remains, rather than producing a report that looks done and is not. It also records the job’s provenance, which data it read and a fingerprint of the job file that read it, and writes it beside the report as dc.gfup.cohort.eda.provenance.json, so the numbers can be traced back later.

Render part of a job

Sometimes a job is half built. The cohort tables are right, but the model below them waits on a corrected variable, and you want a report of what works. The SAS jobs did this by commenting the unfinished part out. Here there are two ways to leave part of a job out, and both keep it visible.

Leave one chunk out with the chunk option skip, giving the reason in quotes:


::: {#tbl-model .cell skip='waiting on the corrected NYHA coding'}

```{.r .cell-code}
...
```
:::

The chunk is neither run nor shown. Use it for a chunk nothing below depends on. If a later chunk needs what the skipped one makes, that later chunk fails; use the next form instead.

Stop the render at a point by calling stop_here() in a chunk on its own:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hvtiRtemplates::stop_here()
```
:::

Everything above it renders; everything below is left out. This suits building a job from the top down, a section at a time.

Both follow the rules the EDIT: markers follow:

  • A draft lists every skip and every stop, by line, in a PARTIAL box at the top of the report, so a partial report cannot pass for a whole one.
  • A final render refuses both. Remove them before render_job(job, final = TRUE).
  • A skip must say why. skip: true with no reason is an error.
  • When you run chunks by hand, stop_here() does nothing, so the chunks below it still run in your session.

When the job stops you

Most stops are the package refusing to guess. The message says what it needs; these are the ones you meet first.

“prefix ‘dc’ carries 3 templates; name one with qualifier, or by its full name.” Several templates share the dc prefix. Use the template’s full name, add_job("dc.gfup", ...), as the call column prints it.

“… already exists; refusing to overwrite.” The job is there already. Open it with open_job() instead of adding it again.

“… is deprecated in favor of …” A warning, not an error: the job is still written. The message names the template that replaces it; use that one for new work.

“N unresolved EDIT: marker(s) remain in this job”, from render_job(final = TRUE). The job is not finished. Find the markers as above, or render a draft to see them listed.

“This job is rendered in part”, from a final render. A skip or stop_here() is still in the job. Remove it, or render a draft instead.

“The figure was not drawn”, in a dc-gfup report. The follow-up figure needs a sensible operation-year column and origin. The box names the problem, usually OPYRS or ORIGIN_YEAR under Study choices. The follow-up tables above it do not depend on the figure, so they are still right.
